overview.title: Training the regularized convnet and its improved learning curves
overview.section: 8.2 Training a convnet from scratch on a small dataset
overview.main_topic: Listing 8.21 trains the dropout convnet on augmented_train_dataset for 100 epochs with checkpointing; Figure 8.11 shows overfitting delayed to epochs 60–70 and validation accuracy above 85%; Listing 8.22 evaluates the best checkpoint on the test set
overview.central_idea: With augmentation and dropout, the gap between training and validation metrics opens much later: around epochs 60–70 instead of epoch 10. Validation accuracy peaks above 85%. The best model by validation loss is checkpointed and then reloaded for an honest test evaluation.
overview.importance: This page quantifies the payoff of the regularization introduced on pp.276–278. It is the evidence that augmentation is worth the trouble, and its test result (83.9%, p.280) closes the from-scratch part of the chapter.
learning_objectives: Explain the role of each ModelCheckpoint argument in Listing 8.21

prerequisites: The dropout convnet of Listing 8.20 and augmented_train_dataset (pp.277–278)

summary:
**Listing 8.21** trains the regularized model from Listing 8.20. A `ModelCheckpoint` callback saves to `convnet_from_scratch_with_augmentation.keras` only when `val_loss` improves (`save_best_only=True`). `model.fit` runs on `augmented_train_dataset` for **100 epochs**, with the unaugmented `validation_dataset` for validation. The callout says: *"Since we expect the model to overfit slower, we train for more epochs."*

The results (**Figure 8.11**) are much better than the baseline's. The authors say overfitting now begins **around epochs 60–70, compared with epoch 10 for the original model**, and validation accuracy **peaks above 85%**, "a big improvement over our first try".

Reading the plot (approximate values):

- **Accuracy.** Training accuracy (dashed red) rises steadily from 0.5 to about 0.95 by epoch 100. Validation accuracy (solid blue) tracks it closely until roughly epoch 40, then levels off and fluctuates in the 0.78–0.87 band.
- **Loss.** Training loss falls almost linearly from about 0.7 to about 0.15. Validation loss falls with it to around 0.4–0.45 and then stops improving, while becoming very noisy. Spikes reach about 0.9 near epoch 42 and about 0.8 near epoch 98.

That noise is exactly why the checkpoint monitors `val_loss` and keeps only the best epoch rather than the last one.

The page ends with **Listing 8.22**, which mirrors Listing 8.17: it reloads the saved best model and evaluates it on `test_dataset`. The result, **83.9%**, appears on the next page (p.280). That is about 5 points above the baseline's 78.6% (p.276).

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s plot the results again; see figure 8.11. Thanks to data augmentation and dropout,
paragraphs.what_it_says: With augmentation and dropout, overfitting starts much later, around epochs 60–70 versus epoch 10 for the original model. Validation accuracy peaks above 85%, a big improvement over the first try.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Regularization lengthened the phase in which training improvements carry over to validation data. In Figure 8.11 the two accuracy curves stay together for about the first 40 epochs. Validation accuracy keeps creeping up in a noisy way until about epoch 90, while validation loss stalls around 0.4 from roughly epoch 40–70 onward and then drifts up with large spikes. The baseline (p.275) had already diverged by epoch 10, with validation accuracy stuck near 80%.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This shows that augmentation plus dropout trade a longer training time for better generalization: about 5–6 points of validation accuracy, and about 5 points of test accuracy (78.6% to 83.9%, pp.276, 280). It also shows that a from-scratch model on 2,000 images still plateaus, which motivates pretrained models (section 8.3).
paragraphs.technical_idea: The jagged validation loss reflects a small validation set (1,000 images) and a sigmoid classifier whose confident mistakes are heavily penalized by binary crossentropy. A few flipped predictions can move the mean loss a lot, even when accuracy barely changes.

concepts.name: ModelCheckpoint with save_best_only
concepts.definition: A Keras callback that saves the model to disk at the end of epochs, optionally only when a monitored metric improves.
concepts.intuition: A "save game" that only overwrites when you reach a new high score.
concepts.technical: With monitor="val_loss" and save_best_only=True, the file always holds the weights from the epoch with the lowest validation loss so far.
concepts.significance: With noisy validation loss and a 100-epoch run, it guarantees you can recover the best epoch instead of the last one.
concepts.misconception: The model object in memory after fit() is the final-epoch model, not the best one. You must reload the file (Listing 8.22).

concepts.name: Overfitting (delayed by regularization)
concepts.definition: Training metrics keep improving while validation metrics stall or worsen.
concepts.intuition: The point where practice stops transferring to the real exam.
concepts.technical: In Figure 8.11 the train/validation gap opens at around epochs 60–70 according to the authors, compared with epoch 10 for the baseline.
concepts.significance: It shows how effective augmentation and dropout are together.
concepts.example: Training accuracy is about 0.95 at epoch 100, while validation is about 0.85.
concepts.misconception: Regularization does not stop overfitting. It postpones it and raises the plateau.

concepts.name: Data augmentation
concepts.definition: Random, label-preserving input transformations applied only at training time.
concepts.intuition: Fresh views of the same images every epoch.
concepts.technical: Here it is applied through augmented_train_dataset, while validation_dataset stays clean.
concepts.significance: Together with dropout, it lifts validation accuracy above 85%.
concepts.misconception: The improvement here is not due to augmentation alone. Dropout was added too.

code.title: Training the regularized ConvNet on augmented images
code.original_code:
callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(
        filepath="convnet_from_scratch_with_augmentation.keras",
        save_best_only=True,
        monitor="val_loss",
    )
]
history = model.fit(
    augmented_train_dataset,
    epochs=100,
    validation_data=validation_dataset,
    callbacks=callbacks,
)
code.what_it_does: Trains the dropout convnet for 100 epochs on augmented training batches, validating on clean images after every epoch and saving the model whenever validation loss reaches a new minimum.

deeper.title: Comparing Figure 8.9 and Figure 8.11
deeper.body:
| | Baseline (p.275) | Augmentation + dropout (this page) |
|---|---|---|
| Epochs trained | 50 | 100 |
| Overfitting begins | about epoch 10 | about epochs 60–70 (per the text) |
| Peak validation accuracy | about 80% | above 85% |
| Final training accuracy | nearly 100% | about 95% (read from plot) |
| Test accuracy | 78.6% (p.276) | 83.9% (p.280) |

The regularized model fits the training set *less* perfectly but generalizes *better*. That is the signature of reduced overfitting.

deeper.title: Why validation loss spikes while validation accuracy does not
deeper.body:
1. Binary crossentropy for one example is $-\log p$ for the correct class.
2. If the model becomes overconfident and wrong on a handful of validation images (say $p = 0.01$), each one contributes $-\log 0.01 \approx 4.6$.
3. Averaged over 1,000 validation images, 50 such mistakes add about 0.23 to the mean loss, even though accuracy falls by at most 5 points.
4. Late in training the model's outputs become more extreme, so these spikes grow. That matches the jagged blue loss curve after epoch 40 in Figure 8.11.
5. That is why choosing the checkpoint by val_loss can pick a different epoch than choosing it by val_accuracy.

deeper.title: A rough-practice analogy
deeper.body: The baseline is a student who memorizes 2,000 flashcards in 10 sessions and then stops improving on new questions. The regularized model studies flashcards that are shuffled, mirrored and partially covered each time. It takes 60–70 sessions to start memorizing, and by then it has learned more of the underlying subject.

misconceptions.correction: It holds the epoch-100 weights. The best ones are in the checkpoint file, which is why Listing 8.22 reloads it.

misconceptions.claim: Peak validation accuracy (>85%) is the expected test accuracy.
misconceptions.correction: Selecting by validation makes it slightly optimistic. The test result is 83.9% (p.280).

misconceptions.claim: The validation-loss spikes mean training diverged.
misconceptions.correction: Training loss keeps falling smoothly. The spikes come from a few overconfident validation errors in a small validation set.

takeaways: The regularized model is trained for 100 epochs on augmented data, with clean validation data and best-val_loss checkpointing.
Overfitting now begins around epochs 60–70 instead of about epoch 10.
Validation accuracy peaks above 85%, up from about 80% for the baseline.
Validation loss becomes very noisy late in training, so checkpointing the best epoch is essential.
Listing 8.22 reloads the best checkpoint for the test evaluation, which gives 83.9% (p.280).

questions.question: According to the authors, when does the regularized model start overfitting?
questions.explanation: The text says "around epochs 60–70 (compared to epoch 10 for the original model)". Epoch 10 is the baseline. The claim that it never overfits is contradicted by the widening gap in Figure 8.11.

questions.question: Why does Listing 8.21 use a different checkpoint filename from the baseline run?
questions.answer: So the best regularized model is saved separately without overwriting convnet_from_scratch.keras, and both can be evaluated and compared (and the new one reused in the next chapter).
questions.explanation: The two listings use distinct filenames. p.280 mentions reusing the augmentation checkpoint later.

questions.question: In Figure 8.11, validation loss is very noisy after about epoch 40 while training loss falls smoothly. How does the training setup protect you from this noise?
questions.answer: ModelCheckpoint with monitor="val_loss" and save_best_only=True keeps the epoch with the lowest validation loss, and Listing 8.22 reloads that checkpoint instead of using the final weights.
questions.explanation: Since the last epoch may fall on a spike (for example the near-0.8 value around epoch 98), selecting the best epoch matters.

questions.question: Which dataset is passed as validation_data in Listing 8.21?
questions.explanation: Augmentation is applied only at training time (p.278). Using the training data or the test set for validation would bias model selection, and augmenting validation data would misrepresent real inputs.

questions.question: The regularized model's final training accuracy (about 95%) is lower than the baseline's (nearly 100%), yet it is the better model. Explain.
questions.answer: Augmentation and dropout make the training task harder and prevent memorization. That lowers training fit but improves generalization, which is what validation and test accuracy measure (above 85% validation, 83.9% test, against about 80% and 78.6%).
questions.explanation: Generalization, not training fit, is the goal. Compare Figure 8.9 (p.275) with Figure 8.11.

questions.question: Can you sketch Figure 8.11 from memory, marking where the accuracy curves separate and where validation loss stops improving, and say how this differs from Figure 8.9?
questions.answer: The accuracy curves stay together until about epoch 40, then validation plateaus at roughly 0.8–0.87 while training climbs to about 0.95. Validation loss bottoms out around 0.4 and turns noisy. In the baseline, separation happened around epoch 10.
